name: blob-object
intent: Records what a Blob costs: one class carrying a large number of fields and operations that have little to do with each other, so the price is that the whole of it must be constructed to use any part of it, its state cannot be reasoned about in pieces, and it resists every reuse and every test.
problem: Attributes and operations accumulate in one class because each new one was added to the class that already existed, so cohesion never got a chance to shape the design. The symptom is quantitative: a disparate collection of unrelated attributes and operations in one class, with an overall lack of cohesiveness between them typical of the blob.
context: The AntiPatterns entry gives the diagnostic threshold and the archetype explicitly: a single class with many attributes and operations — a class with 60 or more attributes and operations usually indicates the presence of the blob — and a single controller class with associated simple, data-object classes, where the controller nearly encapsulates the application's entire functionality much like a procedural main program. It is listed there alongside lack of OO design and a migrated legacy design that was not properly refactored into an OO architecture. DevIQ's framing ties it to God Objects and notes the consequence chain: these classes violate the Single Responsibility and Open/Closed principles, cost more to maintain, and lead to Big Ball of Mud systems. The OO course material gives the same picture from the other side — a small number of classes monopolise processing while the rest just supply data — and the specific origin: in iterative projects, developers add pieces of functionality to an existing working class rather than adding new classes or revising the hierarchy.
benefits: It separates the size problem from the responsibility problem: a class can be large and cohesive, and a blob is specifically the one that is large and not.
The diagnosis is countable, so it can be enforced — 60 or more attributes and operations is the published threshold, and the per-field read count is the structural measurement.
The remedy is one of the cheapest refactorings available: Extract Class, moving each cluster of fields plus the methods that use them, with no behaviour change and no redesign.
It is the intermediate step on the way out of a Big Ball of Mud, because the blob is usually the one class a consolidation pass can attack with a measurable outcome.
tradeoffs: Extraction is easier said than done. The methods that straddle responsibilities are the hard cases — a method that sets one cluster's field from another's value has to be placed, duplicated, or turned into a parameter, and each choice is a design decision.

The published refactoring can produce classes that are small but still unusable if the fields are shared. A field touched by methods across every responsibility becomes a shared 'common' object rather than being eliminated.

The data-object classes that typically surround a blob often have behaviour that should move back to the objects, which is the DevIQ direction (Extract Class so each has a single responsibility) and can mean moving methods in both directions.

There is a threshold argument to make in the other direction: a class that aggregates data for a table or a screen legitimately has many fields, and splitting it purely on count produces a class explosion with no cohesion gain.
The 60-attribute figure is an empirical heuristic from one study of one language, not a law; applying it blindly to a record type or a generated class produces churn.

Persistence frameworks can force the shape. An ActiveRecord entity or a JPA entity carrying serialisation, validation and business rules is a blob, but splitting the persistence type away from the domain type is a change to the framework contract rather than a refactoring.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Testability is the worst axis for a specific reason: constructing the blob means initialising every field, even the ones the test has nothing to do with, so tests grow fixture code in proportion to the blob rather than in proportion to the behaviour. Coupling sits mid rather than high — the blob is heavily referenced, but its own outgoing dependencies are often few because the responsibilities are heterogeneous rather than networked. Performance is mid because a large object has a real construction and memory cost even when it never runs the code under test.

participants.responsibility: The single class holding the disparate attributes and operations; a controller that nearly encapsulates the entire application's functionality.
participants.notes: Diagnosed by count (60+ attributes and operations is the published rule of thumb) and by structure (little cohesiveness between fields and methods).

participants.responsibility: The relatively passive classes the blob holds and manipulates — the items in the catalogue/inventory example that are far-coupled to it.
participants.notes: The intended destination for a large part of the blob's behaviour; the OO course material's refactoring is 'move methods closer to data'.

participants.responsibility: Each unrelated capability that arrived as a method added to the existing working class rather than as a new one.
participants.notes: In iterative projects this is the default outcome, which is why the blob is the normal shape of an untended codebase.

use_cases: A controller class with a dozen data-object fields that does essentially all the processing, while the objects only hold state.
An ActiveRecord model that has accumulated callbacks, validations, associations, formatting and mailer methods until it holds several unrelated responsibilities.
The Catalogue/Item example from the OO course material, where the catalogue is far-coupled to its items and holds both the data and the processing.
A JPA entity carrying persistence, validation, serialisation, authorisation and presentation concerns in one class.
A configuration/settings class that has grown to hold every subsystem's tunables, so it is passed everywhere and every subsystem depends on the whole.
A legacy procedural program ported to classes by wrapping each global in a field, leaving the main loop as a method of the blob.
avoid_when: The class is a deliberate aggregate of a table's columns, a wire record, or a generated binding type — many fields with no behaviour is a record, not a blob.
The class is a framework requirement: an ORM entity, a gRPC message, a configuration bind target, or a state container whose whole job is to hold the set.
The fields genuinely co-vary and are always used together, which is a cohesive data structure rather than a collection of unrelated state.
The operations are few and the fields are many because the domain genuinely has that many inputs — a parser's token table is not a blob.
Splitting would produce classes that each need the whole of the blob's state, in which case the boundary is wrong at a higher level and the fix is architectural.
The class is under active, planned decomposition; a blob on a refactoring branch is an intermediate state, not a smell to report.
pitfalls: Splitting on field count alone, producing a class explosion where each new class has one field and one trivial method.
Extracting the fields and leaving the behaviour behind, which produces a data bag plus a god service rather than two cohesive classes.
Moving methods towards the data and creating a cycle between the extracted class and the blob, which is worse than the original.
Renaming nothing: an extracted class called `BlobPart1` has not been decomposed, it has been catalogued.
Treating a generated or framework-mandated class as a blob and fighting the generator, which will overwrite the split on the next run.
Leaving shared fields behind in a `Common` class referenced by every extracted class, which recreates the blob's coupling under a new name.

related_patterns_notes.god-object: The two are neighbours and the distinction matters: a blob is large because unrelated things accumulated in it, whereas a God Object is large because it became the centre everything routes through. A blob's problem is cohesion; a God Object's is that it became the system's coupling hub.
related_patterns_notes.entity: An entity is deliberately wide — it can have many attributes — and is not a blob because it enforces one invariant and its attributes are cohesive by domain. The boundary is: many attributes and one reason to exist is an entity; many attributes and many reasons is a blob.
related_patterns_notes.value-object: Extract Class is where value objects come from: a group of blob fields with a rule over them becomes a value object with its own equality and its own invariants.
related_patterns_notes.aggregate: A DDD Aggregate can be a large object graph by design and is not a blob when it exists to enforce a consistency boundary; a blob has no boundary, it has a pile.
related_patterns_notes.record-set: A record set / data-object set is exactly what a blob tends to leave behind — the passive data objects the blob does the processing for — so it is both the symptom and half the remedy.
related_patterns_notes.standalone-class: Extract Class is the canonical treatment; the standalone-class condition (a class that does not need the rest of the system) is the acceptance criterion for a successful split.
related_patterns_notes.module: In languages without classes the blob is a module with everything in it, and splitting it is the same operation with module boundaries instead of classes.

anti_patterns: The procedural controller: one class holding the application's main loop and nearly all of its functionality, with passive data objects around it.
The field count rule of thumb breached — 60 or more attributes and operations, with no cohesiveness between them.
Iterative accretion: every feature added a method to the existing working class rather than a new class or a revised hierarchy.
The ActiveRecord model holding validation, callbacks, formatting, authorisation and mailer concerns, so the persistence type cannot be used outside the app.
A configuration class passed to every subsystem because it is easier than passing the three settings each one actually needs.
A ported legacy design: a procedural program wrapped in classes by putting each global into a field and leaving the main loop as a method.
Shared fields extracted into a `Common` object that every extracted class references, recreating the coupling under a new name.
Fields extracted with no behaviour moved, leaving a data bag beside a controller — the blob split down the middle instead of by cohesion.
design_principles: Single responsibility, applied to reasons to change and not to methods: a class with many attributes and many unrelated reasons is many classes with a shared field list.
Cohesion first, size second: a large class whose fields change together is fine; a small class whose fields change for different reasons is not.
Information expert: put each operation with the data it needs; the blob is what results when this rule is inverted for convenience.
Extract Class rather than proliferate methods: cohesion is restored by moving a field together with the methods that use it, not by adding another method to the class that already has everything.
Design for the standalone class: a successful extraction produces classes that need nothing else to be understood or tested.
best_practices: Measure before splitting: count attributes and operations per class (60+ is the published threshold) and count how many methods touch each field; a field read by one method is a candidate for becoming a local variable or moving out entirely.

Group by field usage, not by name: build the internal usage map (which methods touch which fields) and let the clusters define the classes. This is the same technique the Siemens god-class work uses, and it is the one that works on a blob.
Extract Class per cluster, fields and methods together, one cluster per commit, with the build green throughout.
Move methods toward the data as well as data into classes — the OO course material's explicit refactoring for the blob is both directions, and half of it is moving behaviour out to the data objects.
Watch for methods that straddle clusters: they are the real work, and the honest answers are a parameter, a small shared object, or an explicit duplication.
Do not chase the 60 threshold on record types, generated classes or framework bind targets; classify the class first.
After the split, check for a `Common` class holding the fields every cluster touched — that residue is the blob's irreducibly shared state and should be named and bounded, not spread.
Re-measure the same counts after each extraction; the goal is a falling per-class field count and a rising number of fields each method reads from one class, not a smaller file.
sources: AntiPatterns (Bell Labs) Development AntiPattern: The Blob — symptoms (a class with 60 or more attributes and operations; a disparate collection of unrelated attributes and operations; a single controller class with simple data objects; a migrated legacy design), consequences (loss of the OO advantages, too complex to reuse and test, expensive to load), cause (developers add functionality to an existing working class rather than adding new classes or revising the hierarchy), and the refactoring (move behaviour away from the blob, reallocating it to the encapsulated data objects).

DevIQ antipattern catalogue, 'The Blob' — the class that absorbs whatever it touches and grows; similarity to God Objects; violations of SRP and OCP; maintenance cost and the tendency to produce Big Ball of Mud systems; remedy by Extract Class.

SE 350 Object-Oriented Software Development course material, 'The Blob' — the archetype (a small number of classes monopolise processing while the rest provides data), the causes (lack of OO architecture or enforcement, iterative growth without refactoring, ported legacy procedural solution), and the refactoring (move methods closer to data; identify far-coupling such as Catalogue and Item; restructure associations).
Refactoring.guru, Large Class under Bloaters — 'a class contains many fields/methods/lines of code', and the framing that bloaters accumulate over time as the program evolves.
